title: Authentication, signing, authorization and validity are four separate gates on a single operation
content:
## Four questions, four owners

Four concerns all meet at a single operation, and conflating them is the most common source of confusion about what a signature buys you:

| Gate | Question | Where it lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Authentication** | Who is this identity? | Renown |
| **Signing** | Did this identity really produce this exact operation? | Signature verification |
| **Authorization** | Is this identity allowed to perform this action here? | Document permissions |
| **Validity** | Is the resulting state legal? | The reducer |

## What a signature does and does not prove

A signature answers "who, and unchanged?" — authenticity plus integrity. It binds the identity to this specific operation *and its position in the log*, via the stamped `prevOpHash` and `prevOpIndex`.

It does **not** prove:

- that the signer had permission on that document — that is a separate check against document permissions;
- that the change is legal — the reducer still decides;
- that this is the most recent operation — ordering comes from the index and hash chain, not the signature itself.

So a signed operation can be perfectly authentic and still be **rejected**, because the signer lacks permission on that document or because the reducer's rules do not allow the change. Identity establishes *trust*; it does not replace the other checks.

## Why this structure is cheap

None of it needs a bolt-on audit system. Because state is already an ordered, hash-linked log of operations, attaching a signature to each entry is enough to make the whole history **tamper-evident**: change any past operation and every signature and hash after it stops verifying. The same structure that gives deterministic replay and conflict-free sync yields a trustworthy audit trail for free.

> Doc note: the academy section is headed "Three gates, not one" but its table lists four (Authentication, Signing, Authorization, Validity). Four is what the table and the surrounding prose actually describe.

_Source: apps/academy/docs/academy/02-Learn/08-deep-dives/02-identity-and-signing.mdx (Powerhouse v6.2.2-dev.45)._
description: A signature proves who and unchanged — not that the signer had permission, nor that the reducer will accept the change. Each gate has a different owner.
